secrets.kek.heading: The key-encryption key
secrets.kek.what: The key that wraps every data encryption key (#391) — and so protects every signing key, certificate authority, issued key pair, authenticator secret and recovery code, and, in product mode on a postgres store, every row this service mints. Read into this process from a file or a secret store, or kept in a key management service (Vault Transit, AWS KMS, Cloud KMS or Azure Key Vault), which then wraps each data key itself and never hands the key over.
secrets.kek.without: In PRODUCT mode this service does not start without it, and that is deliberate: generating a replacement would stop every token, assertion and signed document it has ever issued from verifying, silently, at somebody else’s relying party. In DEVELOPMENT mode — the default — nothing is persisted, so it is never asked for at all, which is why a perfectly broken configuration can sit here looking fine.
secrets.kek.rotating: Rotated by RE-WRAPPING the data keys, not by re-encrypting the store: put the new key in keys.kek* and the old one in keys.previousKek*, and start. A key rotated inside its key management service needs neither. Never replace it without the previous one beside it: everything wrapped under it would be unreadable, which is why openbao/seed.js refuses to overwrite one.
secrets.database-password.heading: The database password
secrets.database-password.what: The password this service dials PostgreSQL with. It is optional and unconfigured by default, in which case the password is where it has always been — in persistence.databaseUrl, in clear text.
secrets.database-password.without: Nothing, until persistence.mode is postgres. Then this service cannot open its store, and persistence.start() is the one place in this repository where a failure to open something stops the process.
secrets.database-password.rotating: Rotating it is ordinary: change it in the store and in PostgreSQL, and restart. Nothing this service has written depends on its value.
secrets.global-database-password.heading: The global database password
secrets.global-database-password.what: The password this cell dials the GLOBAL tier with — the one writable database every cell shares for realms, settings, applications, policies, signing keys and the routing index, and its replica in this cell (persistence.globalDatabaseUrl, persistence.globalDatabaseReadUrl).
secrets.global-database-password.without: Nothing in single-cell mode. A cell (cells.id set) cannot open the global tier without it where the URL carries none, and a cell with no global tier does not start.
secrets.global-database-password.rotatin: Ordinary: change it in the store and in PostgreSQL, then restart every cell. Nothing written depends on its value.
secrets.cell-kek.heading: This cell's key-encryption key
secrets.cell-kek.what: The AES-256 key the rows RESIDENT in this cell are sealed under — a person's credentials, devices, sessions and everything else minted about the people homed here. It lives only in this cell's region, so another jurisdiction holding a copy of the database still cannot read them. It must not be the service key-encryption key, and is refused if it is.
secrets.cell-kek.without: In PRODUCT mode a cell does not start without it, and there is no fallback to the service key: that would put the people of every jurisdiction under one key. In development mode, and in single-cell mode, it is never asked for.
secrets.cell-kek.rotating: Written once and never replaced, for the same reason as the service key: this service has no re-sealing pass. A person re-homed to another cell is sealed again under THAT cell's key as they move.
secrets.previous-kek.heading: The previous key-encryption key
secrets.previous-kek.what: Read only while the key-encryption key is being ROTATED (#391): the old key, beside the new one in keys.kek*. A data encryption key that unwraps only under the old key is re-wrapped under the new one at start and written back. It may be a key read into this process or a key in a key management service.
secrets.previous-kek.without: none, the default, is the ordinary state. A start with a new key and no previous key, over data keys wrapped under the old one, does not start (STS-KEYS-0091).
secrets.previous-kek.rotating: Set it back to none once every node has started with the new key: by then nothing is wrapped under the old one.
secrets.mail-smtp-password.heading: The SMTP relay password
secrets.mail-smtp-password.what: The SMTP AUTH password (or XOAUTH2 credential) the SMTP mail transport logs in to its relay with, when mail.smtpAuth asks for one.
secrets.mail-smtp-password.without: The SMTP transport cannot log in. In PRODUCT mode a service configured to send through it does not start (STS-MAIL-0002); otherwise each message is a failed attempt and, in the end, a dead letter on Monitoring → Mail.
secrets.mail-smtp-password.rotating: Change it in the store and at the relay. It is read again the next time the transport is built — after any Mail setting changes, or a restart.
secrets.mail-dkim-key.heading: The DKIM private key
secrets.mail-dkim-key.what: The private key of mail.dkimSelector, which common/crypto.js signs every message the SMTP transport sends with (RFC 6376 / RFC 8463).
secrets.mail-dkim-key.without: Nothing, until mail.dkimDomain is set. Then the SMTP transport cannot be built, because a message that should carry a signature and does not fails DMARC at the receiver.
secrets.mail-dkim-key.rotating: Publish the new public key under a NEW selector, point mail.dkimSelector and this secret at it, and withdraw the old record only after mail signed with it has been delivered.
secrets.mail-acs-connection-string.headi: The Azure Communication Services connection string
secrets.mail-acs-connection-string.what: The endpoint and access key the acs mail transport authenticates with, when mail.acsAuth is connection-string. A managed identity needs no secret at all and is the default.
secrets.mail-acs-connection-string.witho: The acs transport cannot be built with connection-string authentication.
secrets.mail-acs-connection-string.rotat: Regenerate the resource’s secondary key, store the string built from it, and regenerate the primary once the transport has been rebuilt.
secrets.mail-gmail-key.heading: The Gmail API service account key
secrets.mail-gmail-key.what: The JSON key of the service account the gmail mail transport signs its token requests with, impersonating mail.gmailSender by domain-wide delegation of the gmail.send scope.
secrets.mail-gmail-key.rotating: Create a second key for the service account, store it, and delete the first once the transport has been rebuilt.
